choices.text: Data drift — the input feature distributions have shifted from what the model was trained on, detectable using Databricks Lakehouse Monitoring with drift metrics
The serving endpoint hardware has degraded, causing numerical precision errors in predictions
The MLflow model artifact has been corrupted and needs to be re-logged from the original training run
The model weights have decayed over time and need to be refreshed by restarting the serving endpoint

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Think about what changes in the real world over time that could cause a static model to become less accurate, even though the model itself has not changed.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Data drift (also called distribution shift) occurs when the statistical properties of the input data change over time relative to the training data. For fraud detection, evolving fraud tactics change the feature distributions that the model encounters. Since the model was trained on historical patterns, it becomes less effective as new patterns emerge. Databricks Lakehouse Monitoring can track feature distributions and model performance metrics over time, alerting when drift exceeds defined thresholds. Model weights do not decay on their own. Hardware does not cause gradual precision changes. Model artifacts stored in MLflow are immutable.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Databricks Lakehouse Monitoring supports drift detection using statistical tests (KS test, chi-squared test) on feature distributions and can generate automated drift reports on Delta tables.
  • Two types of drift matter: data drift (input features change) and concept drift (the relationship between features and the target changes). Both require retraining, but concept drift may also require new features or a different model architecture.
  • Best practice is to set up automated retraining triggers that fire when drift metrics exceed a threshold, creating a closed-loop MLOps pipeline that maintains model freshness.

questions.title: Loading Models from MLflow for Inference
questions.scenario: A data engineer needs to load a trained model from MLflow to generate batch predictions in a Spark job. The model was trained with XGBoost and logged to MLflow. They want to use it as a generic Python function without importing XGBoost directly.
questions.questionText: Which MLflow function loads a logged model as a generic Python callable, regardless of the original training framework?

choices.text: mlflow.pyfunc.load_model(model_uri)
mlflow.xgboost.load_model(model_uri)
mlflow.load_artifact(model_uri)
mlflow.get_run(run_id).data.model

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Consider which MLflow module provides a framework-agnostic interface for loading any logged model as a standard Python function with a predict() method.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: mlflow.pyfunc.load_model() loads any MLflow model (regardless of the original framework — scikit-learn, XGBoost, PyTorch, etc.) as a Python function object with a standard predict() interface. This is MLflow's framework-agnostic model format. mlflow.xgboost.load_model() returns a native XGBoost object, requiring XGBoost to be installed. load_artifact() retrieves generic files, not models. get_run().data does not contain a loadable model object.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• The model_uri can reference models by run ID ("runs:/<run_id>/model"), by registered model name and version ("models:/<name>/<version>"), or by registered model name and stage ("models:/<name>/Production").
  • For batch inference in Spark, use mlflow.pyfunc.spark_udf(spark, model_uri) to wrap the model as a Spark UDF that distributes predictions across the cluster.
  • The pyfunc interface standardizes the predict() method signature: it accepts a pandas DataFrame and returns a pandas DataFrame, Series, or numpy array.

questions.title: MLflow Experiment Tracking Basics
questions.scenario: A data scientist is iterating through different model architectures and hyperparameters to find the best churn prediction model. They want to track the parameters, metrics, and artifacts from each training run so they can compare results and reproduce the best model later.
questions.questionText: Which MLflow component provides a centralized way to log and compare parameters, metrics, and model artifacts across multiple training runs?

choices.text: MLflow Model Registry, which manages model deployment stages
MLflow Projects, which package code for reproducible runs
MLflow Models, which define standard model packaging formats
MLflow Tracking, which records parameters, metrics, and artifacts for each experiment run

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Think about which MLflow component is specifically designed for recording and comparing the results of multiple experiment runs.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: MLflow Tracking is the experiment management component that logs parameters (hyperparameters, configurations), metrics (accuracy, loss, RMSE), and artifacts (model files, plots, data samples) for each training run. Runs are organized into experiments, enabling side-by-side comparison in the MLflow UI. Model Registry manages model versions and lifecycle stages after training. Projects package code for reproducibility. Models defines packaging formats. Tracking is the component used during the experimentation phase.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• In Databricks, each notebook automatically has an associated MLflow experiment. Runs created in that notebook are logged to this experiment by default.
  • Use mlflow.log_param() for individual parameters, mlflow.log_params() for dictionaries, mlflow.log_metric() for metrics (supports step-based logging for training curves), and mlflow.log_artifact() for files.
  • The MLflow Tracking UI provides search, filtering, and visualization of runs, including parallel coordinate plots for understanding hyperparameter-metric relationships.

questions.title: MLflow Autologging
questions.scenario: A data scientist wants to automatically capture all relevant training parameters, metrics, and model artifacts without manually adding mlflow.log_param() and mlflow.log_metric() calls throughout their training code. They use scikit-learn for model training.
questions.questionText: Which MLflow feature automatically captures training parameters, metrics, and model artifacts for supported ML frameworks without requiring explicit logging calls?

choices.text: MLflow Projects with an MLproject configuration file
MLflow autologging, enabled with mlflow.autolog() or mlflow.sklearn.autolog()
MLflow Model Signatures that define input/output schemas
MLflow Recipes that provide pre-built training templates

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Consider which feature intercepts framework training calls and logs parameters, metrics, and models automatically.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: MLflow autologging (mlflow.autolog() or framework-specific variants like mlflow.sklearn.autolog()) automatically instruments supported ML frameworks to log parameters, metrics, and model artifacts without explicit logging calls. For scikit-learn, it captures all estimator parameters, training metrics (accuracy, F1, etc.), and the trained model artifact. In Databricks, autologging is enabled by default for many frameworks. Projects define reproducible code packaging. Signatures describe model input/output schemas. Recipes provide workflow templates.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Autologging is supported for scikit-learn, XGBoost, LightGBM, TensorFlow/Keras, PyTorch Lightning, Spark MLlib, and other frameworks, each with framework-specific captured metrics.
  • In Databricks, autologging is enabled by default via the databricks.automl.autologging configuration, automatically capturing training information even without explicit mlflow.autolog() calls.
  • Autologging can be customized with parameters like log_models (True/False), log_input_examples (True/False), and exclusive (whether to disable other logging), giving control over what is captured.

questions.title: Unity Catalog for ML Governance
questions.scenario: A large enterprise has multiple data science teams building models on the same Databricks workspace. They need centralized governance to control who can access training data, who can register models, and who can deploy models to production. They also need full lineage tracking from data to deployed model.
questions.questionText: Which Databricks component provides unified governance for data, features, models, and ML artifacts across teams?

choices.text: Databricks Workspace access control lists (ACLs) applied to individual notebooks
MLflow Model Registry with stage-based access controls
Cluster-level permissions that restrict which users can run training jobs
Unity Catalog, which provides centralized access control, lineage tracking, and discovery across data assets, feature tables, and registered models

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Think about which component provides a unified governance layer across all asset types — tables, features, and models — with consistent access controls.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Unity Catalog provides centralized governance across all Databricks assets: data tables, feature tables, registered models, volumes (files), and functions. It offers fine-grained access control (GRANT/REVOKE at catalog, schema, and object levels), automated lineage tracking (from source data through features to models), and a searchable discovery interface. Workspace ACLs only cover notebooks. The Workspace Model Registry has limited access controls compared to Unity Catalog's model registry. Cluster permissions do not govern data or model access.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Unity Catalog models are organized in a three-level namespace: catalog.schema.model_name, enabling organizational hierarchies that match team or domain structures.
  • Lineage in Unity Catalog automatically tracks which tables, notebooks, and jobs contributed to each registered model version, enabling impact analysis and compliance auditing.
  • Unity Catalog supports model aliases (e.g., "champion", "challenger") as a more flexible alternative to the Workspace Model Registry's fixed stages (None, Staging, Production, Archived).

questions.title: Reproducibility with MLflow
questions.scenario: A regulatory team asks a data scientist to reproduce a model that was trained six months ago and explain exactly how it was built. The data scientist needs to retrieve the exact code version, data version, hyperparameters, and environment that produced the production model.
questions.questionText: Which combination of MLflow and Databricks features enables full reproducibility of a training run?

choices.text: The notebook revision history alone provides full reproducibility
Only the saved model artifact is needed to reproduce a training run
MLflow run metadata (parameters, code version, data version via Delta time travel) and the logged conda environment together enable full reproducibility
Databricks cluster configuration logs are sufficient to reproduce any model

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Think about what you need to reproduce a training run: the exact data, the exact code, the exact parameters, and the exact software environment.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Full reproducibility requires: (1) hyperparameters — logged by MLflow as run parameters, (2) code version — MLflow logs the git commit hash and notebook revision, (3) data version — Delta Lake's time travel allows reading the exact data version used via timestamps or version numbers, (4) software environment — MLflow logs the conda/pip environment with the model artifact. Together, these capture everything needed to reproduce the training run. The model artifact alone shows what was produced, not how. Notebook history does not capture data versions or parameters. Cluster configuration misses all experiment-specific details.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• MLflow automatically logs the source notebook path, git commit (if available), and source type (notebook or project) with each run, providing code provenance.
  • Log the Delta table version or timestamp as a run tag using mlflow.set_tag("data_version", str(delta_version)) to create an explicit link between the MLflow run and the exact data snapshot.
  • For regulatory compliance, combine MLflow lineage with Unity Catalog's audit logs to provide a complete chain of custody from raw data to production model.

questions.title: CI/CD for ML Pipelines
questions.scenario: A mature ML team wants to automate their model lifecycle: when a data scientist merges new training code into the main branch, it should automatically retrain the model, evaluate it against the current production model, and promote the new version if it meets quality thresholds.
questions.questionText: Which Databricks approach best implements a CI/CD pipeline for automated model retraining and promotion?

choices.text: Schedule a Databricks Workflow that retrains weekly regardless of code changes

Use Databricks Asset Bundles with CI/CD integration that triggers retraining jobs on code merge, compares metrics against the production model, and transitions the model version via the Model Registry API
Manually retrain and promote models using the MLflow UI after each code change
Deploy a separate CI/CD server outside Databricks that SSH-es into the cluster to trigger training

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Think about which approach integrates code versioning, automated testing, and programmatic model promotion into a single automated pipeline.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Databricks Asset Bundles (DABs) define ML resources (jobs, pipelines, model configurations) as code that can be version-controlled and deployed through CI/CD pipelines. When integrated with Git-based CI/CD (GitHub Actions, Azure DevOps, etc.), merging new training code triggers an automated workflow: retrain the model, evaluate against the current production model's metrics, and use the MLflow Model Registry API to promote the new version if it passes quality gates. Scheduled retraining misses code changes. Manual promotion does not scale. External SSH access is a security risk and fragile.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Databricks Asset Bundles use a databricks.yml configuration file that defines jobs, clusters, and permissions as declarative code, enabling infrastructure-as-code for ML pipelines.
  • The CI/CD pipeline typically includes stages: lint/test training code, deploy to a staging workspace, run training on test data, compare metrics with the production model, and promote if quality gates pass.
  • MLflow Model Registry webhooks can trigger downstream actions (like deploying a model to a serving endpoint) when a model version is transitioned to Production, closing the automation loop.

questions.title: MLflow Model Signatures
questions.scenario: A data scientist has logged a model to MLflow but downstream consumers are unsure what input format the model expects. Prediction requests fail because callers pass incorrect column names and data types. The team needs a way to document and enforce the model's expected input and output schemas.
questions.questionText: Which MLflow feature defines and enforces the expected input and output data schemas for a logged model?

choices.text: MLflow Tags, which store arbitrary key-value metadata on runs
MLflow Model Signatures, which specify the input and output column names, types, and shapes
MLflow Artifacts, which store additional files alongside the model
MLflow Parameters, which record the hyperparameters used during training

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Think about which feature serves as a contract between the model and its consumers, defining exactly what data format the model expects and produces.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: MLflow Model Signatures define the schema (column names, data types, and optional shapes for tensor inputs) for both model inputs and outputs. When a signature is saved with the model, MLflow can validate incoming prediction requests and raise errors for schema mismatches before the model runs. This acts as a contract between model producers and consumers. Tags store arbitrary metadata. Artifacts are generic files. Parameters record training hyperparameters, not inference schemas.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Signatures can be inferred automatically from training data using mlflow.models.infer_signature(X_train, y_pred), which captures column names and types from the actual data.
  • When autologging is enabled, MLflow automatically infers and logs the model signature based on the training data and predictions.
  • Model Serving endpoints use the signature to validate incoming REST API requests and return informative error messages when the input does not match the expected schema.

questions.title: Inference Tables for Monitoring
questions.scenario: A production model serving endpoint processes thousands of fraud predictions daily. The team needs to capture every prediction request and response for monitoring, debugging, and compliance. They want to analyze prediction distributions over time to detect data drift and model degradation.
questions.questionText: Which Databricks feature automatically captures model serving request and response payloads for analysis and monitoring?

choices.text: Application logs from the cluster running the serving endpoint
Databricks SQL dashboards that query the model directly
MLflow Tracking, which records metrics from training runs
Inference tables, which automatically log all serving endpoint requests and responses to a Delta table

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Think about which feature provides an automatic, persistent record of every prediction served by a model endpoint.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Inference tables automatically capture every request and response from a Model Serving endpoint into a Delta table. This includes input features, model predictions, timestamps, and endpoint metadata. The captured data can be used for monitoring prediction distributions, detecting data drift, debugging individual predictions, and compliance auditing. Application logs contain system-level information, not structured prediction data. MLflow Tracking records training-time metrics, not serving-time predictions. SQL dashboards are for querying data, not capturing serving events.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Inference tables are stored as Delta tables in Unity Catalog, so they benefit from access controls, lineage tracking, and time travel for historical analysis.
  • Combine inference tables with Lakehouse Monitoring to set up automated drift detection that compares serving-time feature distributions against training-time baselines.
  • Inference tables can be joined with ground truth labels (when they become available) to compute actual model performance metrics, enabling closed-loop monitoring of real-world accuracy.

questions.title: MLflow Run Comparison
questions.scenario: A data scientist has completed 15 experiment runs with different hyperparameter configurations for a classification model. They need to quickly identify which run produced the best F1 score and understand how hyperparameters relate to model performance.
questions.questionText: Which MLflow UI feature allows side-by-side comparison of parameters and metrics across multiple experiment runs?

choices.text: The model registry page, which shows model versions and stages
The run detail page, which shows metrics for a single run only
The artifact browser, which shows files saved with each run
The experiment runs table with sorting, filtering, and the compare runs view with parallel coordinate plots

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Consider which view in the MLflow UI is designed for comparing multiple runs and visualizing parameter-metric relationships across experiments.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: The MLflow experiment page displays all runs in a sortable, filterable table. You can sort by any metric (e.g., F1 score) to find the best run. The "Compare" feature allows selecting multiple runs for side-by-side comparison of parameters and metrics, including parallel coordinate plots that visualize how hyperparameters relate to performance. The model registry shows deployed models, not experiment comparisons. The artifact browser shows files, not metrics. The run detail page is for single-run inspection only.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• The MLflow search API (mlflow.search_runs()) enables programmatic querying of runs using filter expressions like "metrics.f1_score > 0.9 AND params.max_depth = '10'", useful for automated model selection.
  • In Databricks, experiment runs can also be queried as a DataFrame using mlflow.search_runs(experiment_ids=[...]), enabling custom visualizations and analysis in notebooks.
  • Parallel coordinate plots in the compare view help identify parameter ranges that consistently produce good results, guiding more focused hyperparameter search in subsequent experiments.

questions.title: Model Versioning and Aliases
questions.scenario: A data science team manages a recommendation model in Unity Catalog. They want to label the current best-performing model version as "champion" and a newly trained candidate as "challenger" so that serving endpoints and downstream jobs can reference models by these semantic labels rather than version numbers.
questions.questionText: Which Unity Catalog feature allows assigning semantic labels to model versions for easy reference by downstream systems?

choices.text: Model tags, which store arbitrary key-value pairs on model versions
Model aliases, which assign mutable named references (like "champion" or "challenger") to specific model versions
Model comments, which attach text descriptions to model versions
Model schemas, which define the input/output format of model versions

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Think about which feature provides named pointers that can be reassigned from one model version to another, enabling semantic references like "champion."

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Model aliases in Unity Catalog are mutable named references that point to specific model versions. Setting an alias like "champion" on version 5 allows downstream systems to reference "models:/my_model@champion" instead of a version number. When a new version outperforms the current champion, simply reassign the alias to the new version — all downstream references automatically pick up the change. Tags store metadata but are not used for referencing. Comments are descriptive text. Schemas define data formats, not version references.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Aliases replace the Workspace Model Registry's stage concept (None/Staging/Production/Archived) with a more flexible system that supports arbitrary custom labels.
  • You can set aliases programmatically using the MLflow API: client.set_registered_model_alias(name="my_model", alias="champion", version=5).
  • Model Serving endpoints can reference models by alias (e.g., "models:/catalog.schema.model@champion"), enabling zero-downtime model updates by simply moving the alias to a new version.
